title: What It Feels Like to Use Claude (And Why)
description: Claude's narration, refusals and tone explained, plus how to customize Claude Code spinner verbs and when to pick it over ChatGPT or Gemini.
author: freellm.site
content:
Using Claude feels like working with a very articulate colleague who narrates everything they do, occasionally sounds like they think they're smarter than you, and sometimes refuses the task with a polite note about why. A viral r/ChatGPT thread made fun of exactly that mix of vivid narration, strong opinions and low tolerance for unclear intent, and the same mix is why a lot of developers keep Claude open in a second window.

![What It Feels Like to Use Claude (And Why)](/images/blog/what-it-feels-like-to-use-claude/image-0.jpg)

This post looks at where that feel comes from: the spinner verbs people keep screenshotting, the tone that reads as condescending, the refusals, and the worry about tokens that makes people ration it. It also shows how to change the parts you can configure.

## The narration is a real feature

The most-upvoted reaction in that thread was about the words Claude uses to describe what it's doing. In Claude Code, that's the spinner verb, the one-word present participle that ticks by while the model works. The defaults include Thinking, Analyzing and Coding. People screenshot them because now and then one fits absurdly well with what you're debugging.

As one commenter pointed out, you can replace them. Claude Code has a `spinnerVerbs` key in `settings.json` with two modes: `append` (keep the defaults and add yours) or `replace` (use only yours).

```json
{
  "spinnerVerbs": {
    "mode": "append",
    "verbs": [
      "Reticulating splines",
      "Running up that hill",
      "Asking myself how do I work this thing",
      "Folding space",
      "Caffeinating"
    ]
  }
}
```

Put that in `~/.claude/settings.json` for every project on your machine, in `.claude/settings.json` in a repo to share it with a team (commit it), or in `.claude/settings.local.json` for yourself in one repo. Claude Code's [settings precedence docs](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings) explain which file wins when a key is set in more than one place: local overrides project, project overrides user, and managed org settings override everything.

Two practical gotchas:

- This is a fairly recent feature tied to a specific Claude Code version. If you set it and nothing changes, you may be on an older build. Update, then run `claude doctor`, which reports settings it parsed and dropped.
- The setting lives in Claude Code, not in the web or mobile app. People who tried to get custom verbs into the VS Code extension reported that it didn't take. Check the official docs for current support instead of assuming every surface behaves the same.

One widely shared setup replaced the entire default list with hundreds of personal phrases taken from books, philosophy and music, which shows how far `mode: "replace"` can go. While you're in there, two related keys: `spinnerTipsEnabled` (turns off the one-line tip under the spinner) and `statusLine` (runs a shell command to render your own status bar).

## "Claude is like a senior now," and what that costs

Another busy thread settled on a three-tool split that matches how many people work. It deserves attention because it's a routing strategy, not brand loyalty:

| You need | Tool people reach for | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A throwaway question, fast | ChatGPT | Low friction, no need for care |
| Something you could have googled | Gemini | Fast lookup-shaped answers, generous free access |
| Output you'll actually ship | Claude | Holds structure and constraints over long tasks |
| Cheap bulk calls | A free/OSS API tier | See [best free LLM APIs in 2026](/blog/best-free-llm-apis-2026/) |

When people call Claude a "senior engineer," they mean it pushes back, asks about tradeoffs, and won't just agree with a bad plan. The complaints in the same thread are the other side of that. It sometimes sounds condescending, acts as if it knows it's smarter than you, and explains your own question back to you before answering.

The top answers mostly skipped one thing: "feels senior" is a judgment about tone, not a measure of productivity, and the two can diverge. A [Harvard study on Claude Code productivity gains](/blog/harvard-claude-code-productivity-study/) found that measured gains didn't hold up the way people's experience suggested. How confident you feel in the output and how much time it saves are separate questions, so keep them apart when you decide what to pay for.

## The refusals, and why they feel arbitrary

The most substantive complaint in the Claude thread was that it's fragile. It refuses questions that seem harmless, or declines in a way that reads as a judgment of you. Gemini users reported both problems at once: getting blocked by safeguards one moment and finding them ignored the next.

Some of this comes with how safety training works. A model trained to be cautious about a whole category will sometimes catch a harmless example of it, and the same system that decided to refuse also writes the refusal message, so it can sound far more certain about your intent than it should. Things that reduce the friction:

- **Say why.** One sentence about what you're building changes refusal behaviour more than rephrasing does. "I'm writing a security test for my own endpoint" makes a real difference in the prompt.
- **Split the task.** If step three of five is the trigger, ask about steps one and two separately instead of fighting the whole request.
- **Don't argue with the refusal.** Arguing tends to pull the conversation further into the framing that triggered it. Start a new thread and frame it better.
- **Keep a second provider set up.** The same prompt on a different model meets a different policy. An [OpenAI-compatible API](/blog/openai-compatible-api-guide/) makes that a one-line base-URL swap instead of a rewrite.

The thread didn't cover the difference between bans and refusals. A refusal is a decision about one response; action against your account is a policy matter. If you build on Claude commercially, read the usage policies yourself instead of inferring them from forum anecdotes.

## Token anxiety is part of the experience

One of the most candid comments wasn't about quality at all. It was about saving tokens. That's an underrated part of what using Claude feels like: you ration it. You use something cheaper for the simple question so you have room for the hard one, and you keep an internal budget and route around it.

That instinct is right, and it's better to do it deliberately than by feel:

- Use a cheap or free tier for classification, extraction, summarization, and anything where the output is a label rather than prose. A [free LLM API](/blog/best-free-llm-apis-for-coding/) usually handles the boring 80%.
- Save the expensive model for multi-step reasoning, refactors across files, and anything where being subtly wrong costs you.
- Compare actual per-token costs before committing; see [how to compare the cheapest LLM API after the free tier](/blog/cheapest-llm-api-after-free-tier/).
- Check Anthropic's current pricing page for real numbers. Don't trust figures from a forum post, and this post deliberately gives none.

## The parts of the feel that are about you

Two complaints are worth putting side by side. Gemini users complained about excessive flattery, with one saying a newer Gemini release treats them like a genius, a return to 2024-level glazing. Claude users complained about the opposite: too cold, too corrective.

Both describe the same mechanism from opposite ends. These models adapt to the register you write in, which is why [ChatGPT often sounds like you](/blog/why-chatgpt-sounds-like-you/) after a few turns. Write terse, spec-like prompts and Claude answers like a code reviewer. Write exploratory, uncertain prompts and it answers like a tutor, which reads as condescending if you didn't want a tutor. Tightening your prompts is the quickest fix for a tone you dislike, and it's cheaper than switching models.

The narration that started the thread is the same kind of thing: a presentation layer. You can change the verbs, turn off the tips and rewrite the status line. You can't configure away the behaviour of a model trained to explain its reasoning, and for most people who complain about the tone, that explanation is what they're paying for.

If you're deciding how much to build on it, two companion reads: [Claude Made It: vibe-coded mods and the backlash](/blog/claude-made-it-vibe-coded-mods/), on how people receive output when they know a model wrote it, and [AI engineer interviews: how to test AI-assisted coding](/blog/ai-engineer-interview-ai-assisted-coding/), on separating the tool's output from the operator's skill.

## FAQ

### Can I change the words Claude shows while it's thinking?

In Claude Code, yes. Set `spinnerVerbs` in `settings.json` with `"mode": "append"` to add to the defaults or `"mode": "replace"` to swap them out entirely. It's a Claude Code setting, not a web or mobile one; check the current Claude Code docs for which surfaces support it in your version.

### Why does Claude sound condescending?

Mostly because it mirrors the register of your prompt and is trained to explain its reasoning before answering. Terser, more spec-like prompts get terser replies that sound like a peer. There's no tone setting, but the prompt works as one.

### Why does Claude refuse things that seem harmless?

Safety training generalizes across categories, so harmless requests that fall inside a flagged category sometimes get caught. Adding one sentence of legitimate context, or splitting the request so the triggering step is on its own, fixes most cases. Arguing with a refusal usually makes it worse.

### Is Claude actually better than ChatGPT and Gemini?

Users describe routing more than ranking: throwaway questions go to ChatGPT, lookups to Gemini, and work you'll ship to Claude. That's a reasonable default. "Feels better" and "measurably faster" are different claims, though; the Harvard Claude Code study is a case where they diverged.

### How do I use Claude without burning through my budget?

Send the cheap work elsewhere. Classification, extraction and summarization run fine on free tiers, and an OpenAI-compatible endpoint makes switching providers a base-URL change. Check Anthropic's official pricing page for current rates before you plan around any number you read in a forum.
